title_candidates: How close did we come to nuclear war?
Five times one person stopped World War III
What one warhead does to a city
hook: One warhead, one city, ten seconds in. And it nearly happened. At least five times.
topic: Cold War nuclear close calls and what a nuclear war would do

setting.era: the Cold War, 1961-1995, military command posts and early-warning rooms
setting.palette: cold blue-green CRT and radar glow, dark rooms, hard red warning lights, brushed steel and bakelite; outdoors grey winter light
setting.people_style: a Cold War military officer in period uniform, seen from behind or in silhouette, face never clearly visible
setting.negative: recognisable faces of real people, blacked-out or blurred or missing faces, faceless heads, blood, wounds, corpses, injured people, text, writing, letters, numbers, logos, flags with detail, modern smartphones

sources_note: National Security Archive (B-59 2002; 3 a.m. phone call 1979-80); Wikipedia Vasily Arkhipov / 1983 Soviet false alarm / Norwegian rocket incident / 1961 Goldsboro; FAS stockpile 70,300 (1986); NUKEMAP W88 figures via Newsweek 2024; Xia et al. Nature Food 2022 (Rutgers). See research/coldwar_facts.md.

scenes.narration_text: One warhead, one city, ten seconds in. And it nearly happened. At least five times.
scenes.still: a photoreal aerial view of an ANONYMOUS, GENERIC Western-style downtown at dawn — a rectangular street grid of glass office towers, brick mid-rises and parking structures, a river with two bridges, an elevated highway — deliberately unidentifiable: NOT resembling any real city, no East-Asian apartment-block estates, no landmarks, no signs, no text; the camera high and oblique, the whole downtown filling the frame. Over the city centre a boiling orange-black fire column rises, and a perfectly circular ring of grey-white dust — the blast wave — races outward, a third of the way to the frame edge; inside the ring every block is flattened to rubble, outside it the buildings still stand. No people, no text.

setting.era: present day, a simulation
setting.people_style: nobody
setting.palette: photoreal, cinematic; the specific light and colour of each shot is described in the shot itself
setting.negative: recognisable landmarks, people, bodies, injured people, blood, text, letters, numbers, logos, flags

motion.shot: high oblique aerial, wide lens, camera locked, the downtown centred.
motion.b1: the ring is already racing outward; buildings at its edge burst into dust as it hits them.
motion.b2: the ring sweeps across the whole frame, block after block collapsing into grey dust as it passes; windows flash silver; the column above boils higher.
motion.b3: the ring exits the frame; the city inside it a grey plain of rubble.
motion.eye: the ring first, then the collapsing blocks, then the column.
motion.keep: the locked camera and city layout; one ring expanding once; no people; no text
motion.end: the grey plain of rubble under the column.

scenes.narration_text: The last close call wasn't 1962, but 1995. Each time, one person or one switch stopped nuclear war.
scenes.still: Close view of a dark analogue countdown clock on a Cold War console: a round dial with a red sweep hand, a small red lamp beside it lit, brushed-steel panel around it, blurred green CRT light beyond. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels — the dial face is plain with tick marks only. No people.

motion.shot: close view of the dial, medium-long lens, shallow focus, the red hand centred.
motion.b1: the red sweep hand is already ticking; the small lamp beside it glows.
motion.b2: the hand ticks on; the camera pushes in until the dial fills the frame.
motion.b3: the hand stops. Everything still.
motion.eye: the ticking hand first, then the red lamp, then the dial face.
motion.keep: the plain dial with tick marks only, no numbers; the console; nobody
motion.end: the red hand frozen on the dial.

scenes.narration_text: After 1945, two superpowers split the world: America and NATO, the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact.
claims: After the Second World War the world split into a US-led bloc (NATO, founded 1949) and a Soviet-led bloc (the Warsaw Pact, founded 1955).
scenes.still: A dark Cold War situation-room wall display: a flat map of the northern hemisphere in dim lines on black, the Atlantic in the middle — North America on the left and Western Europe glowing a soft BLUE, the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe on the right glowing a soft RED, a thin bright white line running north-south through the middle of Europe where the two colours meet. No text, no labels, no flags, no symbols.

motion.shot: straight-on view of the wall display, medium lens, both blocs in frame.
motion.b1: the blue and red glows are already pulsing faintly, like two breathing lungs.
motion.b2: the white dividing line through Europe brightens; the blue and the red glows pulse harder, pressing against it.
motion.b3: the two colours pressed against the bright line.
motion.eye: the blue bloc first, then the red bloc, then the line between them.
motion.keep: the map, two colours, one line; no text, no labels, no flags
motion.end: the two blocs pressed against the bright line.

scenes.narration_text: They never fought directly. Instead, by 1986: seventy thousand warheads, aimed at each other.
claims: The global nuclear warhead stockpile peaked at about 70,300 in 1986.
scenes.still: A vast underground concrete hall lit by cold strip lights, and in it endless rows of identical dark-grey conical nuclear warheads standing upright on steel cradles, receding into haze, hundreds visible, the rows perfectly regular. No people, no markings, no text.

motion.shot: eye level down the central aisle, wide lens, the rows converging to a vanishing point.
motion.b1: the strip lights are already flickering faintly; the rows stand still.
motion.b2: the camera glides slowly forward down the aisle, warheads sliding past on both sides.
motion.b3: the camera slows, the rows still receding ahead.
motion.eye: the nearest warheads first, then the receding rows, then the haze at the end.
motion.keep: identical warheads, the concrete hall; nobody appears; no text
motion.end: the endless rows receding into haze.

scenes.narration_text: A missile crosses the ocean in thirty minutes. A president gets under ten.
claims: An ICBM flight between Russia and the USA takes about 30 minutes.
Under launch-on-warning a US president may have less than 10 minutes to decide on a nuclear response.
scenes.still: A dark situation-room wall display: a flat world map in dim green on black, North America left, Eurasia right, the Arctic at top; a single thin bright arc drawn from northern Russia over the pole toward the middle of North America, its tip a bright dot. No text, no labels, no borders drawn.

motion.shot: straight-on view of the wall display, medium lens, the whole arc in frame.
motion.b1: the bright dot at the arc's tip is already creeping along the arc toward North America.
motion.b2: the dot crosses the pole and moves on down toward the continent, a faint trail behind it.
motion.b3: the dot is two-thirds of the way, still moving.
motion.eye: the dot first, then the arc, then the dark continent ahead of it.
motion.keep: the map, one arc, one dot; no text, no borders
motion.end: the dot nearing North America.

scenes.narration_text: October 1962. The Soviets secretly put nuclear missiles in Cuba. America blockades the island.
claims: In 1962 the Soviet Union secretly deployed nuclear-armed missiles to Cuba.
In October 1962 the United States imposed a naval blockade, called a quarantine, around Cuba.
Cuba lies about 145 km (90 miles) from Florida.
scenes.still: A dark situation-room wall display: a flat map of the Caribbean in dim green lines on black — the tip of Florida at the top, the long thin island of Cuba across the middle; on Cuba a few small RED dots glowing; around Cuba a wide dashed arc of small bright WHITE dots — ships — curving around the island. No text, no labels, no flags, no borders drawn.

motion.shot: straight-on view of the wall display, medium lens, Florida and Cuba both in frame.
motion.b1: the red dots on Cuba are already pulsing slowly.
motion.b2: the white ship dots creep along the arc, closing the gaps until the dashed line around Cuba is almost solid.
motion.b3: the ring of ships almost closed, the red dots pulsing inside it.
motion.eye: the red dots first, then the ring of ships, then Florida above.
motion.keep: the map, red dots on Cuba, white ship dots; no text, no labels
motion.end: the ring of ships closing around Cuba.

scenes.narration_text: Near the blockade, a Soviet submarine has lost contact with Moscow.
claims: On 27 October 1962 the Soviet submarine B-59 had been out of contact with Moscow for days.
scenes.still: Inside a cramped Soviet diesel submarine control room, 1962, lit only by dim red battle lamps: dripping pipes, brass valves, sweating steel, a periscope well. Exactly two officers in sweat-soaked dark shirts stand at the controls, seen from BEHIND, shoulders hunched, faces not visible. Condensation runs down the bulkheads. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels.

scenes.narration_text: American ships drop practice depth charges to force it up. Inside: forty degrees, no orders.
claims: US Navy ships dropped practice depth charges on B-59 to force it to surface.
B-59's air conditioning had failed and temperatures inside rose above 40 degrees Celsius.
scenes.still: Inside the same red-lit Soviet submarine control room, 1962: exactly two officers seen from BEHIND gripping a rail, heads down. Dust and flakes of paint hang in the air; a hanging lamp swings. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels.

scenes.narration_text: The captain orders the nuclear torpedo readied. Firing needs three officers. Two agree.
claims: B-59 carried a nuclear torpedo.
Firing B-59's nuclear torpedo required the agreement of three senior officers.
scenes.still: Inside the red-lit Soviet submarine, 1962, a TIGHT overhead close-up looking straight DOWN onto the top of a small round brass chart table under one hanging lamp: the table top fills the frame; on the chart lie three brass keys side by side. Entering the frame from three sides are only uniformed FOREARMS and HANDS — no torsos, no shoulders, no heads, no faces, no lamp shade in frame. From the left and from the top, one hand each rests flat on a key; from the right, only the edge of a sleeve at the frame border, its key untouched. Sweat on the sleeves, condensation on the brass. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels.

scenes.narration_text: The third, Vasily Arkhipov, says no. The sub surfaces. Nobody knew until 2002.
claims: Vasily Arkhipov refused to agree to launching B-59's nuclear torpedo and the submarine surfaced.
The B-59 incident became public in 2002.
scenes.still: Night on the open Atlantic, 1962: a black Soviet submarine's conning tower breaking the surface, water sheeting off it, and on top exactly one officer in a dark coat and cap, seen from BEHIND, small against a grey-black sea and low cloud; far off, the searchlights of two warships as pale smears. No faces, no text.

scenes.narration_text: Three a.m., June 1980. The phone rings beside President Carter's security adviser.
claims: On 3 June 1980 National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski was woken around 3 a.m. by a call reporting a Soviet missile launch.
scenes.still: A dark bedroom in Washington, 1980: a beige rotary telephone on a bedside table under a small warm lamp that has just been switched on, and behind it exactly one man of about fifty in a dressing gown sitting on the edge of the bed, seen from BEHIND, his hand reaching for the receiver. Cold moonlight through a window. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels.

motion.keep: exactly one man seen only from behind; the lamp, the phone, the window; no face; no text
motion.end: the man frozen with the receiver at his ear.

scenes.narration_text: America's warning computers: two hundred Soviet missiles incoming. A second call: over two thousand.
claims: During the 3 June 1980 NORAD false alarm, displays reported first about 200 and then about 2,000 incoming Soviet missiles.
scenes.still: The NORAD operations centre inside Cheyenne Mountain, 1980: a huge wall display showing a dim outline of North America in green on black, and across the top of the continent a dense swarm of hundreds of tiny bright dots arcing down from the north; rows of empty consoles glowing amber below; red alert lamps along the ceiling. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels. No people.

motion.b2: more dots pour in from the top edge, the swarm thickening; the camera pushes in on the map.
motion.b3: the map fills the frame, the dots still coming.
motion.eye: the swarm first, then the flashing red lamps, then the empty consoles.
motion.keep: the map, the dots, the empty consoles; no people; no text or numbers
motion.end: the map dark with dots.

scenes.narration_text: He doesn't wake his wife; everyone dies in half an hour. One minute before calling the president—
claims: Brzezinski did not wake his wife during the 1980 false alarm, reasoning that everyone would be dead within half an hour.
Brzezinski was about one minute from calling President Carter when the alarm was cancelled.
scenes.still: A dark study in Washington, 1980: exactly one man in a dressing gown standing at a desk, seen from BEHIND, one hand flat on the desk, the other holding a beige telephone receiver halfway between the cradle and his ear; a desk lamp; a window with cold moonlight; a closed door to the bedroom behind him. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels.

motion.b3: the hand and receiver frozen, filling the frame.

scenes.narration_text: —the phone rings again. Nothing is coming. A forty-six-cent chip was inventing missiles.
claims: The June 1980 NORAD false alarm was caused by a faulty computer chip costing 46 cents.
scenes.still: Extreme close-up of a small black 1970s integrated-circuit chip with metal legs, lying alone on a green circuit board, one leg slightly discoloured, under hard cold light; the board's traces soft in the background. No text or markings on the chip. No people.

scenes.narration_text: September 1983. Midnight in a Soviet bunker near Moscow. Sirens. The screen: American missile launch.
claims: On 26 September 1983 the Soviet early-warning system at Serpukhov-15 reported a US missile launch shortly after midnight.
scenes.still: The Serpukhov-15 early-warning bunker, 1983: a long dim room of consoles facing a giant wall map of the northern hemisphere in dark green — a PLAIN map: coastlines only, absolutely NO place names, NO labels, NO lettering, NO country names printed on it — and above the map one huge rectangular red panel glowing bright, blank, with no writing; exactly one officer in uniform seen from BEHIND standing up from his chair at the central console. Red rotating lamps along the ceiling. no legible text, letters or numbers anywhere on screens or panels.

scenes.narration_text: One American missile, then five. Protocol says report it. Above him, they would launch.
claims: The 1983 Serpukhov-15 alarm reported one US missile and then four more, five in total.

No people.

scenes.narration_text: Petrov thinks: a real attack means hundreds. Radar shows nothing. He calls it a malfunction.
claims: Stanislav Petrov judged the 1983 alarm to be false because a real US first strike would involve hundreds of missiles, and ground radar showed nothing.

scenes.narration_text: Sunlight on high clouds. He was right. His reward: a reprimand, and early retirement.
claims: The 1983 Soviet false alarm was caused by sunlight reflecting off high-altitude clouds.
After the 1983 incident Petrov received no reward, was reprimanded over paperwork and later took early retirement.

scenes.narration_text: On Russian radar it looks like an American Trident missile. For the first time, the nuclear briefcase opens.
claims: Russian early-warning radar interpreted the 1995 Norwegian rocket as resembling a US Trident submarine-launched missile.
In the 1995 Norwegian rocket incident the Russian nuclear briefcase (Cheget) was activated for the first known time.

scenes.narration_text: Ten minutes to decide. Eight pass. Then the track turns out to sea. Norway's warning never arrived.
claims: Russian officers had about 10 minutes to decide on a response to the 1995 Norwegian rocket and spent about 8 of them tracking it.
Norway had notified Russia of the 1995 rocket launch in advance but the notice never reached the Russian military.

No people.

scenes.narration_text: 1961: an American B-52 breaks up over North Carolina, dropping two hydrogen bombs. One switch holds.
claims: In January 1961 a B-52 broke up over Goldsboro, North Carolina, dropping two Mark 39 hydrogen bombs.
A 1969 Sandia memo concluded that on one of the Goldsboro bombs three of four safety mechanisms failed and a single low-voltage switch prevented detonation.

scenes.narration_text: Every time, one officer, one switch, one call said no. What if nothing had?

scenes.narration_text: One warhead. Four hundred fifty-five kilotons. Above a city of eight million.
claims: The US W88 submarine-launched warhead has a yield of about 455 kilotons.

scenes.narration_text: Now a full exchange between America and Russia: thousands of warheads. Every major city on two continents burns.
